name: Rice domestication in the Middle Ganges plain
summary: People of the Middle Ganges plain used, and perhaps cultivated, wild rice from about 6400 BCE; fully domesticated rice is dated there to about 1800 to 1600 BCE.
description: Charred rice grains from Lahuradewa, in the Middle Ganges plain of northern India, are radiocarbon dated to about 6400 BCE; their excavators called them domesticated, but later study found that they overlap with wild grains and may mark the start of a long cultivation of wild rice. The earliest dated fully domesticated rice in the region, identified from spikelet bases, is at Mahagara, about 1800 to 1600 BCE, close to the time when East Asian japonica rice is thought to have arrived and hybridised with the local rice. The cited study argues from Indus sites further west that domestication was already under way in northern South Asia before that arrival.

impact.note: Rice became the staple grain of the Ganges plain and of much of South Asia for millennia (reach 2) and the basis of how those people fed themselves (depth 3), with later work mostly refining its cultivation (generativity 1); the reach is from general knowledge, not the cited paper.

date.label: c. 1800–1600 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Domesticated rice, identified from spikelet bases, is dated at Mahagara in the Middle Ganges region to about 1800 to 1600 BCE.

evidence.supports: Until recently the earliest evidence for domesticated rice based on spikelet base evidence was from the site of Mahagara in the same region, c.1800–1600 BCE

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Lahuradewa: charred rice grains are radiocarbon dated to 6409 BCE (8359 cal BP) by Tewari et al. (2008), as quoted by Bates et al.; whether they were domesticated, cultivated wild rice or gathered is disputed (Fuller et al. 2010). The event was left out so that a disputed wild-rice date does not become the record's date.
No site coordinates were in the source, so the place is the Middle Ganges plain with approximate coordinates.
Whether the north Indian rice tradition was independent of japonica, and the c. 2000 BCE arrival date, need Fuller (2011), which was not opened.

research.note: Bates et al. quote Fuller's view that the north Indian rice tradition did not reach full domestication on its own before japonica arrived about 2000 BCE, and argue against it from Indus sites, so independence is unsettled.
